claim: Neuromodulators promote adaptive behaviors that are often complex and involve concerted activity changes across circuits that are often not physically connected.
source: Neuromodulators promote adaptive behaviors that are often complex and involve concerted activity changes across circuits that are often not physically connected.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuromodulators based on established scientific understanding.

claim: The Caenorhabditis elegans NLP-12 neuropeptide system shapes responses to food availability by modulating the activity of head and body wall motor neurons through alternate G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) targets, CKR-1 and CKR-2.
source: Here, we show that the Caenorhabditis elegans NLP-12 neuropeptide system shapes responses to food availability by modulating the activity of head and body wall motor neurons through alternate G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) targets, CKR-1 and CKR-2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ckr-2 deletion reduces body bend depth during movement under basal conditions.
source: We show ckr-2 deletion reduces body bend depth during movement under basal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CKR-1 is a functional NLP-12 receptor.
source: We demonstrate CKR-1 is a functional NLP-12 receptor and define its expression in the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Biased CKR-1 GPCR stimulation of head motor neurons promotes turning during local searching.
source: In contrast to basal locomotion, biased CKR-1 GPCR stimulation of head motor neurons promotes turning during local searching.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and behavioral data presented in Figures 3, 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Deletion of ckr-1 reduces head neuron activity and diminishes turning.
source: Deletion of ckr-1 reduces head neuron activity and diminishes turning while specific ckr-1 overexpression or head neuron activation promote turning.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 8 and behavioral data in Figure 3.

claim: Specific ckr-1 overexpression promotes turning.
source: Deletion of ckr-1 reduces head neuron activity and diminishes turning while specific ckr-1 overexpression or head neuron activation promote turning.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Head neuron activation promotes turning.
source: Deletion of ckr-1 reduces head neuron activity and diminishes turning while specific ckr-1 overexpression or head neuron activation promote turning.
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Locomotor responses to changing food availability are regulated through conditional NLP-12 stimulation of head or body wall motor circuits.
source: Thus, our studies suggest locomotor responses to changing food availability are regulated through conditional NLP-12 stimulation of head or body wall motor circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Disruptions in neuromodulatory transmitter systems are associated with eating disorders, anxiety, stress and mood disorders, depression, and schizophrenia.
source: Disruptions in neuromodulatory transmitter systems are associated with a variety of behavioral and neuropsychiatric conditions, including eating disorders, anxiety, stress and mood disorders, depression, and schizophrenia (Bailer and Kaye, 2003; Kormos and Gaszner, 2013; Pomrenze et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neuropeptide Y (NPY) coordinates a variety of energy and feeding-related behaviors in mammals through circuit-specific mechanisms.
source: For example, Neuropeptide Y (NPY) coordinates a variety of energy and feeding-related behaviors in mammals through circuit-specific mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NPY signaling may increase or decrease food intake depending upon the circuit and GPCR targets involved.
source: NPY signaling may increase or decrease food intake depending upon the circuit and GPCR targets involved (West and Roseberry, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: C. elegans NLP-12 neuropeptides are key modulatory signals in the control of behavioral adaptations to changing environmental conditions, such as food availability or oxygen abundance.
source: Prior work has shown that C. elegans NLP-12 neuropeptides are key modulatory signals in the control of behavioral adaptations to changing environmental conditions, such as food availability or oxygen abundance (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Hums et al., 2016; Oranth et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NLP-12 system is the closest relative of the mammalian Cholecystokinin (CCK) neuropeptide system and is highly conserved across flies, worms, and mammals.
source: The NLP-12 system is the closest relative of the mammalian Cholecystokinin (CCK) neuropeptide system and is highly conserved across flies, worms, and mammals (Janssen et al., 2009; Janssen et al., 2008; Peeters et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The C. elegans genome encodes two putative CCK-responsive G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (CKR-1 and CKR-2).
source: Like mammals, the C. elegans genome encodes two putative CCK-responsive G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (CKR-1 and CKR-2), though, prior to the present study, direct activation by NLP-12 peptides had only been demonstrated for the CKR-2 GPCR (Frooninckx et al., 2012; Janssen et al., 2009; Janssen et al., 2008; Peeters et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on genomic information and prior literature.

claim: Prior to the present study, direct activation by NLP-12 peptides had only been demonstrated for the CKR-2 GPCR.
source: Like mammals, the C. elegans genome encodes two putative CCK-responsive G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (CKR-1 and CKR-2), though, prior to the present study, direct activation by NLP-12 peptides had only been demonstrated for the CKR-2 GPCR (Frooninckx et al., 2012; Janssen et al., 2009; Janssen et al., 2008; Peeters et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sudden decreases in food availability or environmental oxygen levels each evoke a characteristic behavioral response in C. elegans where animals limit their movement to a restricted area by increasing the frequency of trajectory changes (reorientations), a behavior known as local or area-restricted searching (ARS).
source: Sudden decreases in food availability or environmental oxygen levels each evoke a characteristic behavioral response in C. elegans where animals limit their movement to a restricted area by increasing the frequency of trajectory changes (reorientations), a behavior known as local or area-restricted searching (ARS) (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2005; Hills et al., 2004; Hums et al., 2016; Oranth et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ARS is a highly conserved adaptive behavior and is evident across diverse animal species.
source: ARS is a highly conserved adaptive behavior and is evident across diverse animal species (Bailey et al., 2019; Bell, 1990; Marques et al., 2020; Paiva et al., 2010; Sommerfeld et al., 2013; Weimerskirch et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Trajectory changes increase within a few minutes after food removal, and decrease with prolonged removal from food (>15–20 min) as animals transition to global searching (dispersal).
source: Trajectory changes increase within a few minutes after food removal, and decrease with prolonged removal from food (>15–20 min) as animals transition to global searching (dispersal) (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Calhoun et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2005; Hills et al., 2004; Hums et al., 2016; Oranth et al., 2018; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NLP-12 neuropeptide signaling promotes increases in body bending amplitude and turning during movement.
source: NLP-12 neuropeptide signaling promotes increases in body bending amplitude and turning during movement (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Hums et al., 2016), motor adaptations that are particularly relevant for ARS.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: nlp-12 is strongly expressed in only a single neuron, the interneuron DVA that has synaptic targets in the motor circuit and elsewhere.
source: Notably, nlp-12 is strongly expressed in only a single neuron, the interneuron DVA that has synaptic targets in the motor circuit and elsewhere (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; White et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ckr-2 deletion (tm3082) has been characterized previously and likely represents a null allele.
source: The ckr-2 deletion (tm3082) has been characterized previously and likely represents a null allele (Hu et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2008; Peeters et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ckr-1 deletion (ok2502) removes 1289 base pairs, including exons 3–7 that encode predicted transmembrane domains 2–5.
source: The ckr-1 deletion (ok2502) removes 1289 base pairs, including exons 3–7 that encode predicted transmembrane domains 2–5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C) and therefore also likely represents a null allele.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The ckr-1 deletion (ok2502) likely represents a null allele.
source: The ckr-1 deletion (ok2502) removes 1289 base pairs, including exons 3–7 that encode predicted transmembrane domains 2–5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C) and therefore also likely represents a null allele.
evidence: This is inferred from the extent of the deletion.

claim: ckr-1 and ckr-2 single gene deletions each partially reversed the effects of nlp-12 overexpression.
source: ckr-1 and ckr-2 single gene deletions each partially reversed the effects of nlp-12 overexpression (Figure 1A,B,D, 6C), indicating that both CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs are active under conditions when NLP-12 peptides are present at high levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A, B, D, and 6C.

claim: Both CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs are active under conditions when NLP-12 peptides are present at high levels.
source: ckr-1 and ckr-2 single gene deletions each partially reversed the effects of nlp-12 overexpression (Figure 1A,B,D, 6C), indicating that both CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs are active under conditions when NLP-12 peptides are present at high levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic suppression data.

claim: ckr-1 deletion showed slightly greater suppression of nlp-12(OE) phenotypes compared with ckr-2 deletion.
source: Notably, ckr-1 deletion showed slightly greater suppression of nlp-12(OE) phenotypes compared with ckr-2 deletion (Figure 1B,D, 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, D, and 6C.

claim: Combined deletion of ckr-1 and ckr-2 largely reversed the locomotor changes produced by NLP-12 overexpression.
source: Combined deletion of ckr-1 and ckr-2 largely reversed the locomotor changes produced by NLP-12 overexpression (Figure 1A,B,D, 6C), indicating that the GPCRs act in a partially redundant manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A, B, D, and 6C.

claim: CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs act in a partially redundant manner.
source: Combined deletion of ckr-1 and ckr-2 largely reversed the locomotor changes produced by NLP-12 overexpression (Figure 1A,B,D, 6C), indicating that the GPCRs act in a partially redundant manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic suppression data.

claim: Application of either NLP-12–1 or NLP-12–2 synthetic peptides produced robust calcium responses in cells expressing CKR-1.
source: Application of either NLP-12–1 or NLP-12–2 synthetic peptides produced robust calcium responses in cells expressing CKR-1.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NLP-12–1 activates CKR-1 with an EC50 of 3.5 nM.
source: These responses were concentration-dependent with EC50 values of 3.5 and 1.9 nM for NLP-12–1 and NLP-12–2 peptides, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NLP-12–2 activates CKR-1 with an EC50 of 1.9 nM.
source: These responses were concentration-dependent with EC50 values of 3.5 and 1.9 nM for NLP-12–1 and NLP-12–2 peptides, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NLP-12–1 activates CKR-2 with an EC50 of 8.0 nM.
source: These EC50 values are comparable to those measured for NLP-12 activation of CKR-2 (8.0 nM and 10.2 nM) (Figure 1F; Janssen et al., 2008), suggesting NLP-12 peptides act with similar potency across CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: NLP-12–2 activates CKR-2 with an EC50 of 10.2 nM.
source: These EC50 values are comparable to those measured for NLP-12 activation of CKR-2 (8.0 nM and 10.2 nM) (Figure 1F; Janssen et al., 2008), suggesting NLP-12 peptides act with similar potency across CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: NLP-12 peptides act with similar potency across CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs.
source: These EC50 values are comparable to those measured for NLP-12 activation of CKR-2 (8.0 nM and 10.2 nM) (Figure 1F; Janssen et al., 2008), suggesting NLP-12 peptides act with similar potency across CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of EC50 values.

claim: No other peptides from a library of over 350 synthetic C. elegans peptides elicited CKR-1 activation.
source: Importantly, no other peptides from a library of over 350 synthetic C. elegans peptides elicited CKR-1 activation, nor did the NLP-12 peptides evoke calcium responses in cells transfected with empty vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that CKR-1, like CKR-2, is a highly specific receptor for NLP-12.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NLP-12 peptides did not evoke calcium responses in cells transfected with empty vector.
source: Importantly, no other peptides from a library of over 350 synthetic C. elegans peptides elicited CKR-1 activation, nor did the NLP-12 peptides evoke calcium responses in cells transfected with empty vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that CKR-1, like CKR-2, is a highly specific receptor for NLP-12.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro calcium response assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CKR-1, like CKR-2, is a highly specific receptor for NLP-12.
source: Importantly, no other peptides from a library of over 350 synthetic C. elegans peptides elicited CKR-1 activation, nor did the NLP-12 peptides evoke calcium responses in cells transfected with empty vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that CKR-1, like CKR-2, is a highly specific receptor for NLP-12.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity data.

claim: nlp-12 deletion significantly reduced both body bending and head bending angles in comparison to wild type.
source: nlp-12 deletion significantly reduced both body bending and head bending angles in comparison to wild type (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Single deletions in ckr-1 and ckr-2 each produced significant reductions in body bending.
source: Similarly, single deletions in ckr-1 and ckr-2 each produced significant reductions in body bending, and combined deletion produced effects similar to nlp-12 deletion (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Combined deletion of ckr-1 and ckr-2 produced effects on body bending similar to nlp-12 deletion.
source: Similarly, single deletions in ckr-1 and ckr-2 each produced significant reductions in body bending, and combined deletion produced effects similar to nlp-12 deletion (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Head bending was strikingly affected by ckr-1 deletion.
source: In contrast, head bending was strikingly affected by ckr-1 deletion, while ckr-2 deletion did not produce a significant reduction (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ckr-2 deletion did not produce a significant reduction in head bending.
source: In contrast, head bending was strikingly affected by ckr-1 deletion, while ckr-2 deletion did not produce a significant reduction (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of nlp-12 significantly decreased reorientations immediately following removal from food.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Bhattacharya et al., 2014), we found that deletion of nlp-12 significantly decreased reorientations immediately following removal from food (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: nlp-12 deletion significantly reduced forward reorientations, but had no appreciable effect on reversal-coupled omega turns.
source: In particular, we noted a significant reduction in the forward reorientations of nlp-12 mutants, but no appreciable effect on reversal-coupled omega turns (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Deletion of ckr-2 produced no appreciable effect on reorientations.
source: Deletion of ckr-2 produced no appreciable effect on reorientations (Figure 3C–D; Bhattacharya et al., 2014); however, single deletion of ckr-1 decreased reorientations to a similar level as observed for nlp-12 deletion (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Single deletion of ckr-1 decreased reorientations to a similar level as observed for nlp-12 deletion.
source: Deletion of ckr-2 produced no appreciable effect on reorientations (Figure 3C–D; Bhattacharya et al., 2014); however, single deletion of ckr-1 decreased reorientations to a similar level as observed for nlp-12 deletion (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: ckr-1 deletion significantly impacted forward reorientations, but did not affect reversal-coupled omega turns.
source: Similar to nlp-12(lf), we found that ckr-1(lf) significantly impacted forward reorientations, but did not affect reversal-coupled omega turns (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Combined deletion of ckr-1 and ckr-2 provided no additional decrease in reorientations beyond that observed for single ckr-1 deletion.
source: Combined deletion of ckr-1 and ckr-2 provided no additional decrease beyond that observed for single ckr-1 deletion (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Combined deletion of nlp-12 and ckr-1 did not further decrease reorientations compared with either of the single mutants.
source: In addition, combined deletion of nlp-12 and ckr-1 did not further decrease reorientations compared with either of the single mutants (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Expression of wild-type ckr-1, but not ckr-2, rescued reorientations in ckr-1(lf);ckr-2(lf) double mutants.
source: Expression of wild-type ckr-1, but not ckr-2, rescued reorientations in ckr-1(lf);ckr-2(lf) double mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Expression of wild-type ckr-1 restored normal reorientation behavior in ckr-1(lf) animals when expressed under the control of native ckr-1 promoter elements (3.5 kb).
source: Expression of wild-type ckr-1 also restored normal reorientation behavior in ckr-1(lf) animals when expressed under the control of native ckr-1 promoter elements (3.5 kb) (Figure 3C), but not when expressed under the ckr-2 promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of wild-type ckr-1 under the ckr-2 promoter did not restore normal reorientation behavior in ckr-1(lf) animals.
source: Expression of wild-type ckr-1 also restored normal reorientation behavior in ckr-1(lf) animals when expressed under the control of native ckr-1 promoter elements (3.5 kb) (Figure 3C), but not when expressed under the ckr-2 promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: nlp-12 and ckr-1 act in the same genetic pathway.
source: These findings show that nlp-12 and ckr-1 act in the same genetic pathway and point to a selective requirement for NLP-12 signaling through CKR-1 in regulating trajectory changes during local searching.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis data.

claim: There is a selective requirement for NLP-12 signaling through CKR-1 in regulating trajectory changes during local searching.
source: These findings show that nlp-12 and ckr-1 act in the same genetic pathway and point to a selective requirement for NLP-12 signaling through CKR-1 in regulating trajectory changes during local searching.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and behavioral data.

claim: Deletion of nlp-12 did not produce significant changes in dispersal behavior.
source: Deletion of nlp-12 did not produce significant changes in dispersal behavior, but we noted a modest decrease in reorientations during dispersal in ckr-1 mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was a modest decrease in reorientations during dispersal in ckr-1 mutants.
source: Deletion of nlp-12 did not produce significant changes in dispersal behavior, but we noted a modest decrease in reorientations during dispersal in ckr-1 mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Animals reorient more frequently with depolarization of DVA compared to pre-stimulus control.
source: We found that animals reorient more frequently with depolarization of DVA compared to pre-stimulus control (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Light exposure did not increase reorientations in the absence of retinal (–ATR).
source: Importantly, light exposure did not increase reorientations in the absence of retinal (–ATR) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Depolarization of the DVA neuron in nlp-12 mutants failed to produce enhancement of reorientations.
source: Depolarization of the DVA neuron in nlp-12 mutants failed to produce a similar enhancement (Figure 3F), offering support for the idea that reorientations primarily arise due to the release of NLP-12 peptides.
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Reorientations primarily arise due to the release of NLP-12 peptides from DVA.
source: Depolarization of the DVA neuron in nlp-12 mutants failed to produce a similar enhancement (Figure 3F), offering support for the idea that reorientations primarily arise due to the release of NLP-12 peptides.
evidence: This is inferred from the photostimulation experiments.

claim: Single ckr-1 deletion or combined ckr-1 and ckr-2 deletion abrogated DVA-elicited increases in reorientation behavior.
source: Single ckr-1 deletion or combined ckr-1 and ckr-2 deletion also abrogated DVA-elicited increases in reorientation behavior, while single ckr-2 deletion produced more variable responses that were not clearly distinguishable from control (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Single ckr-2 deletion produced more variable responses to DVA photostimulation that were not clearly distinguishable from control.
source: Single ckr-1 deletion or combined ckr-1 and ckr-2 deletion also abrogated DVA-elicited increases in reorientation behavior, while single ckr-2 deletion produced more variable responses that were not clearly distinguishable from control (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: NLP-12 release from the DVA neuron promotes reorientation behavior.
source: Our photostimulation experiments provide direct evidence that NLP-12 release from the DVA neuron promotes reorientation behavior, and, in addition, provide evidence for central involvement of NLP-12 signaling through the CKR-1 GPCR in directing reorientations.
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: NLP-12 signaling through the CKR-1 GPCR is centrally involved in directing reorientations.
source: Our photostimulation experiments provide direct evidence that NLP-12 release from the DVA neuron promotes reorientation behavior, and, in addition, provide evidence for central involvement of NLP-12 signaling through the CKR-1 GPCR in directing reorientations.
evidence: This is supported by photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: NLP-12 expression has been recently reported in PVD neurons.
source: While NLP-12 expression has also been recently reported in PVD neurons (Tao et al., 2019), expression of nlp-12 under a PVD specific promoter (ser-2prom3) did not restore reorientations in nlp-12(lf) animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), pointing toward DVA as the primary source of NLP-12 in promoting reorientations.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Expression of nlp-12 under a PVD specific promoter (ser-2prom3) did not restore reorientations in nlp-12(lf) animals.
source: While NLP-12 expression has also been recently reported in PVD neurons (Tao et al., 2019), expression of nlp-12 under a PVD specific promoter (ser-2prom3) did not restore reorientations in nlp-12(lf) animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), pointing toward DVA as the primary source of NLP-12 in promoting reorientations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: DVA is the primary source of NLP-12 in promoting reorientations.
source: While NLP-12 expression has also been recently reported in PVD neurons (Tao et al., 2019), expression of nlp-12 under a PVD specific promoter (ser-2prom3) did not restore reorientations in nlp-12(lf) animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), pointing toward DVA as the primary source of NLP-12 in promoting reorientations.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claim: ckr-1 overexpression produced striking increases in turning and large head to tail body bends.
source: We found that ckr-1 overexpression produced striking increases in turning and large head to tail body bends (Figure 4A, 6C, Video 4), qualitatively similar to the effects of nlp-12 overexpression (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 6C.

claim: ckr-1(OE) animals made steep bends during runs of forward movement, with angles approaching 200°.
source: ckr-1(OE) animals made steep bends during runs of forward movement, with angles approaching 200°, whereas bending angles in wild type rarely exceeded 75° (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Bending angles in wild type rarely exceeded 75°.
source: ckr-1(OE) animals made steep bends during runs of forward movement, with angles approaching 200°, whereas bending angles in wild type rarely exceeded 75° (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The amplitude of body bends during movement increased by approximately threefold in ckr-1(OE) animals compared to wild type.
source: The amplitude of body bends during movement also increased by approximately threefold in ckr-1(OE) animals compared to wild type (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increases in bending angles and body bend depth in ckr-1(OE) animals were returned to wild-type levels by nlp-12 deletion.
source: These increases in bending angles and body bend depth were returned to wild-type levels by nlp-12 deletion (Figure 4A–C), offering support that NLP-12 peptides are the major CKR-1 ligands required to elicit these characteristic changes in movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: NLP-12 peptides are the major CKR-1 ligands required to elicit characteristic changes in movement.
source: These increases in bending angles and body bend depth were returned to wild-type levels by nlp-12 deletion (Figure 4A–C), offering support that NLP-12 peptides are the major CKR-1 ligands required to elicit these characteristic changes in movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic suppression data.

claim: ckr-1 is broadly expressed in the nervous system, showing expression in a subset of ventral nerve cord motor neurons, amphid and phasmid sensory neurons, premotor interneurons, and motor neurons in the nerve ring.
source: We found that ckr-1 is broadly expressed in the nervous system, showing expression in a subset of ventral nerve cord motor neurons, amphid and phasmid sensory neurons, premotor interneurons, and motor neurons in the nerve ring (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: In the ventral nerve cord, ckr-1 is expressed in cholinergic, but not GABAergic, ventral cord motor neurons.
source: In the ventral nerve cord, we found that ckr-1 is expressed in cholinergic, but not GABAergic, ventral cord motor neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The ckr-1 reporter is expressed in GABAergic RMEV, RMED, AVL and RIS neurons, cholinergic SMDV, SMDD, and RIV head motor neurons, the interneuron RIG, the serotonergic NSM neuron, and in the interneurons AIA and AIB.
source: Amongst head neurons, the ckr-1 reporter is expressed in GABAergic RMEV, RMED, AVL and RIS neurons, cholinergic SMDV, SMDD, and RIV head motor neurons, the interneuron RIG, the serotonergic NSM neuron, and in the interneurons AIA and AIB (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: ckr-1 is expressed in the amphid sensory neurons ASK and ASI and the phasmid sensory neurons PHA and PHB.
source: Additional studies using DiI uptake indicated that ckr-1 is also expressed in the amphid sensory neurons ASK and ASI and the phasmid sensory neurons PHA and PHB (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by DiI uptake studies.

claim: With the exception of the ventral cord cholinergic neurons, the ckr-1 reporter almost exclusively labeled neurons that do not receive direct synaptic input from DVA.
source: With the exception of the ventral cord cholinergic neurons, the ckr-1 reporter almost exclusively labeled neurons that do not receive direct synaptic input from DVA, suggesting that NLP-12 acts at least partially through extrasynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This is based on comparison of ckr-1 expression with known DVA connectivity.

claim: NLP-12 acts at least partially through extrasynaptic mechanisms.
source: With the exception of the ventral cord cholinergic neurons, the ckr-1 reporter almost exclusively labeled neurons that do not receive direct synaptic input from DVA, suggesting that NLP-12 acts at least partially through extrasynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of ckr-1.

claim: ckr-1 and ckr-2 expression showed little overlap.
source: Notably, ckr-1 and ckr-2 expression showed little overlap (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transgenic strains where pan-neuronally expressed ckr-1 (rgef-1 promoter) was injected at high concentration displayed increased body bending amplitude.
source: Transgenic strains where pan-neuronally expressed ckr-1 (rgef-1 promoter) was injected at high concentration displayed increased body bending amplitude, similar to overexpression using the native promoter (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ectopic ckr-1 expression in muscles produced no appreciable change in body bending amplitude.
source: In contrast, ectopic ckr-1 expression in muscles produced no appreciable change, consistent with a primary site of CKR-1 action in neurons (Figure 5C).

claim: The primary site of CKR-1 action is in neurons.
source: In contrast, ectopic ckr-1 expression in muscles produced no appreciable change, consistent with a primary site of CKR-1 action in neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of muscle-specific expression.

claim: ckr-1 overexpression in cholinergic (unc-17β promoter) or GABAergic (unc-47 promoter) ventral nerve cord motor neurons did not elicit an appreciable change in body bend depth.

claim: ckr-1 overexpression using either the odr-2(16) or lgc-55 promoters produced a striking (2.5-fold) increase in body bend depth.
source: ckr-1 overexpression using either the odr-2(16) or lgc-55 promoters produced a striking (2.5-fold) increase in body bend depth, comparable with ckr-1 overexpressed under its endogenous promoter.

claim: ckr-1 overexpression in GABAergic neurons, including RMED and RMEV (unc-47 promoter), did not produce an appreciable effect on body bend depth.
source: In contrast, ckr-1 overexpression in GABAergic neurons, including RMED and RMEV (unc-47 promoter), did not produce an appreciable effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ckr-1 overexpression in RIV, RIG, NSM, AIA, AIB, or amphid neurons failed to significantly enhance body bend depth.
source: Likewise, ckr-1 overexpression in RIV, RIG, NSM, AIA, AIB, or amphid neurons failed to significantly enhance body bend depth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The lgc-55 promoter drives expression in AVB, RMD, SMD, and IL1 neurons, as well as neck muscles and a few other head neurons.
source: The lgc-55 promoter drives expression in AVB, RMD, SMD, and IL1 neurons, as well as neck muscles and a few other head neurons (Pirri et al., 2009), while the odr-2(16) promoter primarily labels the RME and SMD head neurons (Chou et al., 2001; Supplementary files 2-3).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The odr-2(16) promoter primarily labels the RME and SMD head neurons.
source: The lgc-55 promoter drives expression in AVB, RMD, SMD, and IL1 neurons, as well as neck muscles and a few other head neurons (Pirri et al., 2009), while the odr-2(16) promoter primarily labels the RME and SMD head neurons (Chou et al., 2001; Supplementary files 2-3).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NLP-12::Venus clusters in the nerve ring region of the DVA process are concentrated in the vicinity of SMD processes.

claim: The four SMDs (dorsal-projecting SMDDL and SMDDR and ventral-projecting SMDVL and SMDVR) are bilateral motor neuron pairs that innervate dorsal and ventral head/neck musculature, and also form reciprocal connections with one another.
source: The four SMDs (dorsal-projecting SMDDL and SMDDR and ventral-projecting SMDVL and SMDVR) are bilateral motor neuron pairs that innervate dorsal and ventral head/neck musculature, and also form reciprocal connections with one another (White et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SMD neurons have been previously implicated in directional head bending and steering.
source: They have been previously implicated in directional head bending and steering (Gray et al., 2005; Hendricks et al., 2012; Kaplan et al., 2020; Kocabas et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2016; Yeon et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Animals overexpressing ckr-1 under control of the odr-2(16) promoter showed significant increases in body bending amplitude and bending angle compared to wild type.
source: For both overexpression strains, we observed significant increases in body bending amplitude and bending angle compared to wild type (Figures 5C and 6A–C, Video 5).

claim: Animals overexpressing ckr-1 under control of the flp-22∆4 promoter showed significant increases in body bending amplitude and bending angle compared to wild type.
source: For both overexpression strains, we observed significant increases in body bending amplitude and bending angle compared to wild type (Figures 5C and 6A–C, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 6A-C.

claim: Increases in body bending amplitude and bending angle from SMD-specific ckr-1 overexpression were dependent on NLP-12 signaling.
source: These increases were dependent on NLP-12 signaling (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and were similar to those observed for native ckr-1 (Figures 4 and 6C, Video 4) and nlp-12 overexpression (Figures 1 and 6C, Video 1).

claim: The actions of CKR-1 in the SMD motor neurons recapitulate many of the behavioral effects of NLP-12 overexpression.
source: Thus, the actions of CKR-1 in the SMD motor neurons recapitulate many of the behavioral effects of NLP-12 overexpression.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes.

claim: Following photoactivation of miniSOG in animals overexpressing ckr-1, striking decreases in bending angles and amplitude during movement were observed.
source: Following photoactivation of miniSOG in animals overexpressing ckr-1, we observed striking decreases in bending angles (Figure 6D–E) and amplitude (Figure 6F) during movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D-F.

claim: SMD motor neurons are required for the locomotor effects of ckr-1 overexpression.
source: These results indicate that SMD motor neurons are required for the locomotor effects of ckr-1 overexpression, and, importantly, raise the possibility that the SMD neurons are key targets for NLP-12 neuromodulation during local searching in wild type.
evidence: This is inferred from the SMD ablation experiments.

claim: The SMD neurons are key targets for NLP-12 neuromodulation during local searching in wild type.
source: These results indicate that SMD motor neurons are required for the locomotor effects of ckr-1 overexpression, and, importantly, raise the possibility that the SMD neurons are key targets for NLP-12 neuromodulation during local searching in wild type.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: SMD-specific expression of wild-type ckr-1 restored reorientations during food searching to roughly wild-type levels in ckr-1 mutants.
source: However, expression in ckr-1 mutants restored reorientations during food searching to roughly wild-type levels (Figure 7A), indicating that CKR-1 function in the SMD neurons is sufficient to support NLP-12 modulation of local searching.

claim: CKR-1 function in the SMD neurons is sufficient to support NLP-12 modulation of local searching.
source: However, expression in ckr-1 mutants restored reorientations during food searching to roughly wild-type levels (Figure 7A), indicating that CKR-1 function in the SMD neurons is sufficient to support NLP-12 modulation of local searching.

claim: Following the onset of photostimulation, Chrimson-expressing animals rapidly increased reorientations.
source: Following the onset of photostimulation, Chrimson-expressing animals rapidly increased reorientations (Figure 7B–C, Video 6), while control animals (-Retinal) did not increase trajectory changes during the light stimulation period (Figure 7C).

claim: Control animals (-Retinal) did not increase trajectory changes during the light stimulation period.
source: Following the onset of photostimulation, Chrimson-expressing animals rapidly increased reorientations (Figure 7B–C, Video 6), while control animals (-Retinal) did not increase trajectory changes during the light stimulation period (Figure 7C).

claim: SMD photostimulation elicited a modest increase in body bending.
source: SMD photostimulation also elicited a modest increase in body bending (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Transient and inducible silencing of the SMDs by histamine-gated chloride channel expression significantly reduced reorientations during food searching.
source: Conversely, transient and inducible silencing of the SMDs by histamine-gated chloride channel expression significantly reduced reorientations during food searching (Figure 7D).

claim: Direct activation or inhibition of SMD neurons alter turning and reorientations.
source: Thus, direct activation or inhibition of SMD neurons alter turning and reorientations, consistent with a potential mechanism for NLP-12/CKR-1 modulation of local searching through signaling onto the SMD neurons.

claim: A striking elevation of wild-type SMD activity during ARS compared with dispersal was observed.

claim: Overall calcium levels during ARS were positively correlated with reorientation frequency.
source: Though overall calcium levels during ARS were positively correlated with reorientation frequency (Figure 8D, Pearson's correlation r=0.54), discrete events where the peak fluorescence ratio was elevated were not well correlated with specific episodes of behavior.

claim: Discrete events where the peak fluorescence ratio was elevated were not well correlated with specific episodes of behavior.
source: Though overall calcium levels during ARS were positively correlated with reorientation frequency (Figure 8D, Pearson's correlation r=0.54), discrete events where the peak fluorescence ratio was elevated were not well correlated with specific episodes of behavior.

claim: SMD activity of ckr-1(lf) animals remained low throughout the ARS period.
source: By comparison, SMD activity of ckr-1(lf) animals remained low throughout the ARS period (Figure 8C–E), supporting a model (Figure 9) where NLP-12/CKR-1 signaling promotes local searching by biasing SMD head motor neurons toward increased activation.

claim: NLP-12/CKR-1 signaling promotes local searching by biasing SMD head motor neurons toward increased activation.
source: By comparison, SMD activity of ckr-1(lf) animals remained low throughout the ARS period (Figure 8C–E), supporting a model (Figure 9) where NLP-12/CKR-1 signaling promotes local searching by biasing SMD head motor neurons toward increased activation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Under basal conditions, NLP-12 modulation of the body wall motor circuit predominates, influencing the depth of body bends during sinusoidal movement through CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs located on body wall motor neurons.
source: Under basal conditions, we suggest that NLP-12 modulation of the body wall motor circuit predominates, influencing the depth of body bends during sinusoidal movement through CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs located on body wall motor neurons.

claim: NLP-12 activation of head motor neurons through CKR-1 becomes predominant in the absence of food, promoting reorientations.
source: NLP-12 activation of head motor neurons through CKR-1 becomes predominant in the absence of food, promoting reorientations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Changes in food availability reconfigure functional connectivity in the NLP-12 system by differentially engaging GPCRs across the head and body wall motor circuits.
source: We propose that changes in food availability reconfigure functional connectivity in the NLP-12 system by differentially engaging GPCRs across the head and body wall motor circuits.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: The involvement of two GPCRs in nematode NLP-12 signaling is reminiscent of the organization of the CCK system in rodents, which relies on signaling through CCK1 and CCK2 GPCRs.
source: Intriguingly, the involvement of two GPCRs in nematode NLP-12 signaling is reminiscent of the organization of the CCK system in rodents, which relies on signaling through CCK1 and CCK2 GPCRs (Janssen et al., 2009).

claim: NLP-12 neuropeptides act as key modulators in a range of C. elegans behaviors.
source: NLP-12 neuropeptides act as key modulators in a range of C. elegans behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement based on prior literature.

claim: Local search responses to varying oxygen levels and decreased food availability both involve NLP-12 signaling.
source: Local search responses to varying oxygen levels and decreased food availability both involve NLP-12 signaling (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Hums et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NLP-12 signaling has been implicated in various aspects of proprioceptive signaling and postural control.
source: Additionally, NLP-12 signaling has been implicated in various aspects of proprioceptive signaling and postural control (Hu et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reorientations during searching are produced through high angle forward turns and reversal-coupled omega turns.
source: Reorientations during searching are produced through high angle forward turns (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Broekmans et al., 2016; Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999) and reversal-coupled omega turns (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of nlp-12 has modest effects on body posture during normal exploratory movement.
source: Our analysis here shows that loss of nlp-12 also has modest effects on body posture during normal exploratory movement, indicating NLP-12 regulation of motor targets under basal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The behavioral requirement for NLP-12 is far more apparent during local searching compared with basal locomotion.
source: Intriguingly, the behavioral requirement for NLP-12 is far more apparent during local searching compared with basal locomotion, suggesting enhanced involvement of NLP-12 signaling for performance of local searching.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Enhanced involvement of NLP-12 signaling is suggested for performance of local searching.
source: Intriguingly, the behavioral requirement for NLP-12 is far more apparent during local searching compared with basal locomotion, suggesting enhanced involvement of NLP-12 signaling for performance of local searching.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Increased engagement of head motor neurons through CKR-1 activation may be a generalizable mechanism for dynamic NLP-12 regulation of behavior over changing external conditions.
source: Based on our observations, we speculate that increased engagement of head motor neurons through CKR-1 activation may be a generalizable mechanism for dynamic NLP-12 regulation of behavior over changing external conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: CKR-2 shows slightly broader expression compared with CKR-1.
source: CKR-2 shows slightly broader expression compared with CKR-1, but both GPCRs are expressed across a variety of neuron classes, including many that do not receive direct synaptic inputs from DVA.

claim: Both CKR-1 and CKR-2 GPCRs are expressed across a variety of neuron classes, including many that do not receive direct synaptic inputs from DVA.
source: CKR-2 shows slightly broader expression compared with CKR-1, but both GPCRs are expressed across a variety of neuron classes, including many that do not receive direct synaptic inputs from DVA.

claim: The two GPCRs serve distinct roles in modulating behavior.
source: We noted very little overlap in CKR-1 and CKR-2 expression, consistent with the idea that the two GPCRs serve distinct roles in modulating behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns.

claim: NLP-12 activation of CKR-2 stimulates neurotransmission through coupling with egl-30 (Gαq) and egl-8 (PLCβ) likely by DAG interaction with the synaptic vesicle priming factor UNC-13.
source: NLP-12 activation of CKR-2 stimulates neurotransmission through coupling with egl-30 (Gαq) and egl-8 (PLCβ) likely by DAG interaction with the synaptic vesicle priming factor UNC-13 (Hu et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It seems likely that CKR-1 also functions to positively regulate neuronal activity through egl-30.
source: Given the sequence homology between CKR-1 and CKR-2, it seems likely that CKR-1 also functions to positively regulate neuronal activity through egl-30.
evidence: This is speculated based on sequence homology.

claim: SMD-specific CKR-1 overexpression and SMD neuron photostimulation produced qualitatively similar behavioral effects.
source: In support of this idea, we found that SMD-specific CKR-1 overexpression and SMD neuron photostimulation produced qualitatively similar behavioral effects.

claim: The DVA neuron makes a single synapse with SMDVL.
source: The DVA neuron makes a single synapse with SMDVL (Worm wiring).
evidence: This is based on known connectivity data.

claim: It seems likely that extrasynaptic signaling to other SMD neurons also contributes to NLP-12 elicited behavioral changes during local searching.
source: While it is possible that this single synapse accounts for NLP-12 elicited behavioral changes during local searching, it seems likely that extrasynaptic signaling to other SMD neurons also contributes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the expression patterns and behavioral data.

claim: Prior studies have indicated SMDs are cholinergic and their stimulation is sufficient to produce Ca2+ transients in head/neck muscles.
source: Prior studies have indicated SMDs are cholinergic and their stimulation is sufficient to produce Ca2+ transients in head/neck muscles, consistent with proposed roles in head bending (Pereira et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2016).

claim: Prior studies noted anti-phasic activity between SMDD and SMDV neurons and opposing head/neck musculature during head bending (or head casting).

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Physiological regulation of SMD activity is complex and involves reciprocal connections with RIA interneurons, reciprocal signaling with RME motor neurons, as well as proprioceptive feedback.
source: Physiological regulation of SMD activity is complex and involves reciprocal connections with RIA interneurons, reciprocal signaling with RME motor neurons, as well as proprioceptive feedback (Hendricks et al., 2012; Ouellette et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2016; White, 2018; White et al., 1997; Yeon et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitory signaling from the GABAergic RME neurons onto the SMDs is implicated in modulation of head bending amplitude to optimize head bends for forward movement.
source: In particular, inhibitory signaling from the GABAergic RME neurons onto the SMDs is implicated in modulation of head bending amplitude to optimize head bends for forward movement.
evidence: This is based on prior literature.

claim: One intriguing possibility is that NLP-12-elicited increases in SMD activity uncouple the SMDs from RME inhibitory regulation, perhaps promoting large amplitude head swings that couple to forward reorientations during searching.
source: While the precise role of NLP-12 modulation of SMD activity remains unclear, one intriguing possibility is that NLP-12-elicited increases in SMD activity uncouple the SMDs from RME inhibitory regulation, perhaps promoting large amplitude head swings that couple to forward reorientations during searching.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Elevated SMD activity is permissive for reorientations to occur.
source: We propose that elevated SMD activity is permissive for reorientations to occur, perhaps acting in concert with SMD proprioceptive functions (Yeon et al., 2018) or other neurons implicated in the regulation of head movement and turning, such as SMB (Oranth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Recent work suggests an interesting functional coupling between the activity of SMD neurons and ventral cord B-type motor neurons.
source: Recent work suggests an interesting functional coupling between the activity of SMD neurons and ventral cord B-type motor neurons (Kaplan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

source: B-type motor neurons are suggested to act as a distributed central pattern generator for the propagation of body bends (Gao et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: CKR-1 activation of SMDs may therefore influence body depth directly by altering body wall motor neuron excitability through a gap junction connection between VB1 and SMDVR or through neuromuscular synapses located in the sub-lateral processes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on known connectivity.

claim: Differential contributions of CKR-1 and CKR-2 during basal locomotion and search responses do not arise due to dramatic differences in NLP-12 potency to activate each receptor.
source: The similar potency of NLP-12 peptides for activating CKR-1 and CKR-2, suggests that differential contributions of these GPCRs during basal locomotion and search responses do not arise due to dramatic differences in NLP-12 potency to activate each receptor.

claim: NLP-12 regulation of the SMD neurons acts in parallel with other neural pathways previously shown to promote reversals during local searching.
source: We envision that NLP-12 regulation of the SMD neurons acts in parallel with other neural pathways previously shown to promote reversals during local searching.
evidence: This is a proposed model.

claim: The SMD neurons receive synaptic information from the olfactory circuit (e.g., through synaptic connections from the AIB and RIM neurons).

claim: A pathway activated by food removal may enhance SMD sensitivity to CKR-1 activation.
source: The SMD neurons also receive synaptic information from this circuit (e.g., through synaptic connections from the AIB and RIM neurons) (White et al., 1997), raising the possibility that a pathway activated by food removal may enhance SMD sensitivity to CKR-1 activation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: SMD neurons may be a site for integration of information encoding reversals and forward reorientations during local searching.
source: In this case, SMD neurons may be a site for integration of information encoding reversals and forward reorientations during local searching.

source: A shift to CKR-1 modulation of head neurons during searching could also be triggered by dopaminergic stimulation of DVA.

claim: Prior work implicated dopaminergic signaling from PDE neurons in the regulation of NLP-12 and motor responses.
source: Prior work implicated dopaminergic signaling from PDE neurons in the regulation of NLP-12 and motor responses (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Oranth et al., 2018).

claim: PDE regulates an antagonistic peptidergic circuit, mediated by FLP-1 neuropeptides, through inhibitory connections with AVK interneurons.
source: Notably, PDE also regulates an antagonistic peptidergic circuit, mediated by FLP-1 neuropeptides, through inhibitory connections with AVK interneurons (Oranth et al., 2018), suggesting potentially more distributed behavioral regulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The NLP-12 system conditionally engages GPCRs expressed in head or body motor neurons to modify specific features of locomotion.
source: We propose that the NLP-12 system conditionally engages GPCRs expressed in head or body motor neurons to modify specific features of locomotion, most notably reorientations during searching and body bend depth during basal locomotion.

claim: Brain CCK has been increasingly implicated as a key regulator in diverse aspects of behavior, including feeding, satiety, memory, nociception, and anxiety.
source: Brain CCK has been increasingly implicated as a key regulator in diverse aspects of behavior, including feeding, satiety, memory, nociception, and anxiety (Ballaz, 2017; Chandra and Liddle, 2007; Liddle, 1997; Miyasaka and Funakoshi, 2003; Lajtha and Lim, 2006; Rehfeld, 2017).
